description: Without bees, **75% of the world's food crops** would be in danger. These small, inconspicuous workers support our food supply, and their populations are collapsing.

hero.hook: They don't just make honey: without them, a large part of our food would disappear.

blocks.text: We often think of bees only for their honey. In reality, they provide a much greater service: they allow the majority of flowering plants to reproduce. This service is worth hundreds of billions of dollars every year.

In recent decades, these essential insects have been disappearing at a worrying speed. Understanding their role and the causes of their decline allows us to better understand a direct issue for our future food supply.

is the transport of pollen, the male cells of one flower, to the female organ of another flower of the same species. Wind or water can sometimes do this, but the majority of flowering plants prefer animal transport. By searching for nectar and pollen for their colony, bees provide this transport without even knowing it. [[pollination]]

blocks.caption: While foraging, the bee carries pollen from flower to flower.

blocks.text: A bee can visit up to 700 flowers per day. To produce just 500 grams of honey, an entire colony must fly the equivalent of three times around the Earth.

About **75% of the world's food crops** depend, at least somewhat, on pollinators like bees. This includes coffee, cocoa, apples, almonds or avocados. The contribution of pollination to the global economy is estimated between $235 billion and $577 billion per year.

sections.title: Pollination, a discreet but essential job

blocks.text: The decline of bees does not have a single cause: several threats act at the same time. Since the 1990s, some beekeepers have lost up to 30 to 50% of their colonies each winter, while natural loss should be around 10%. This phenomenon of sudden disappearance is sometimes called . [[Colony collapse disorder]]

blocks.caption: Neonicotinoids penetrate the entire plant, including nectar and pollen.

blocks.text: , a family of insecticides, are particularly responsible. They permeate the entire plant, including its nectar and pollen. Even at low doses, they disorient the bees, who can no longer find their hive, and weaken their immune system. [[Neonicotinoids]]

Added to this are a parasitic mite which transmits deadly viruses, the disappearance of wild flowers due to monocultures, and climate change, which shifts flowering periods in relation to the awakening of insects.

When we say “bee”, we almost always think of the domestic bee, the one that lives in hives and produces honey. However, it is only one species among more than **20,000** in the world, including bumblebees and osmia. Most are solitary and do not make honey, but play an equally important ecological role.
Certain flowers, like those of the tomato, only release their pollen under a specific vibration. Honeybees don't know how to do this, but bumblebees do, thanks to a technique called sonication.

These wild species are often specialized on a specific plant, which they are sometimes the only ones able to pollinate effectively. They are also more vulnerable than the domestic bee, because they do not benefit from any human monitoring or care. Their disappearance weakens the entire , since many birds depend on the fruits and seeds resulting from this pollination. [[food chain]]

sections.title: There is not just one bee

blocks.text: Reducing the use of pesticides remains the most effective lever. The European Union banned three major neonicotinoids in open fields in 2018. At the same time, putting back in place , such as hedges or flower strips, recreates refuge areas for insects. [[agroecological infrastructures]]
Everyone can also act simply: planting local flowers in their garden or leaving their lawn a little longer before mowing it offers a real refuge for bees when flowers are rare.
Protecting pollinators is not just a matter of preserving nature: it is a long-term survival strategy, since their work directly supports the ability of plants to feed us.

Bees and 20,000 species of wild pollinators ensure the reproduction of 75% of the world's food crops. Their decline, caused by pesticides, parasites and habitat loss, directly threatens our food supply.

title: Why are bees vital?
